li.a: NPR: Here's what we know so far about the deadly attack in New Orleans
CBS News: New Orleans truck attacker identified as Army veteran from Texas who declared support for ISIS, officials say
NBC News: New Orleans attack truck driver identified as Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a Texas-based Army veteran
ABC News: Truck-ramming suspect used wrong device in failed detonation of IEDs, officials say
WGNO, published by Yahoo News: FBI provides update on fatal Bourbon Street attack investigation
Fox News: Bourbon Street terrorist researched Germany attack before deadly rampage, FBI says
ABC News: Super Bowl honors victims, first responders of New Orleans terror attack
Fox 8 WVUE: Fox 8 looks back at the 2025 Bourbon Street terror attack, and ahead to what's next

content.p: In the early hours of New Year's Day 2025, a man drove a rented pickup truck down the middle of Bourbon Street in New Orleans, through a crowd of revellers celebrating in the French Quarter. Fourteen people died. Police said dozens were injured. After the truck stopped, the driver climbed out and fired on officers and was shot dead.

The FBI identified the attacker as Shamsud-Din Jabbar, who was 42, lived in Houston, Texas, and had served in the Army, and it investigated the attack as terrorism. Because he died at the scene there was no prosecution, and what the public knows comes from the FBI's briefings, press accounts and the local reviews that followed. The bureau said it had seen no indication of an accomplice and, according to a briefing aide, found no evidence that he had been directed by anyone else.

At about 3:15 a.m., according to New Orleans police, the driver veered around a police vehicle that was blocking the intersection of Canal and Bourbon streets, went up onto the sidewalk and then back onto Bourbon. NPR reported that he continued for almost three blocks, crossing Iberville and Bienville streets, before crashing just short of Conti Street. Fox 8 reported that the truck hit a piece of construction equipment. Police Superintendent Anne Kirkpatrick said he had driven at "a very fast pace" and was trying to "run over as many people as he possibly could". "This was intentional," she said.
After the crash he got out and shot at officers, wounding two of them. Police returned fire and killed him. The two officers were released from hospital on the Thursday, CBS News reported.

The death toll was first given by the FBI as 15 people, not counting the driver. On 2 January the New Orleans coroner's office revised it to 14, saying the earlier figure had included the attacker. Reports of the number injured varied: 35 in the FBI's first count, 30 in an NBC report on the day, and "more than 50" in a later local account. The FBI's update in mid-January put it at 57, with 136 victims identified, including two businesses that suffered damage.

Fox 8 spoke to relatives and friends of two of those killed. Latasha Polk was remembered by a friend as "a beautiful person". Nicole Perez was a mother whose own mother, Marta Perez, spoke of telling her grandson that his mother was gone. Another of the dead was 27-year-old Martin "Tiger" Bech, whose friend Ryan Quigley was injured in the attack. The Philadelphia Eagles later gave Quigley two Super Bowl tickets; he said he had promised his friend he would take him if the team made it.

Jabbar was born and raised in Beaumont, Texas, according to a video for one of his real estate businesses, which NPR quoted. NBC News reported that he attended Georgia State University and graduated with a degree in computer information systems, and that Deloitte, which confirmed he had worked for it since 2021, said it was shocked to learn of the link. The Army spokesperson told NPR that he served from March 2007 to January 2015 and then in the Army Reserve until July 2020, with about 11 months in Afghanistan from February 2009. NBC, citing defense officials, gave his active service as 2006 to 2015. He left as a staff sergeant, honorably discharged. NBC also reported that Texas records showed he was charged with misdemeanour theft in 2002 and with driving with an invalid licence in 2005.

A childhood friend, Chris Pousson, told NBC that the person he knew had been quiet and reserved and that the attack was "a complete 180". His younger brother, Abdur-Rahim Jabbar, said in an interview with CBS News that over the preceding year Shamsud-Din had become more devout, dressing more modestly, removing his tattoos and giving up alcohol, but that the family had seen no sign of radicalisation. In early 2024 Jabbar posted recordings online describing music as the "voice of Satan", CBS reported, though he said nothing then about violence.
content.h2: What the FBI says about motive
content.p: The FBI said an Islamic State flag was attached to the truck's hitch. Christopher Raia, deputy assistant director of its counterterrorism division, said that shortly before the attack Jabbar posted several videos online proclaiming his support for ISIS, and that he had written on Facebook that he joined the group the previous summer. In one video, Raia said, he declared that he had planned to attack family and friends but worried the headlines would not focus on what he called a "war between the believers and the disbelievers". Raia also said it was not clear why Jabbar chose Bourbon Street.

On 2 January the FBI said it did not assess that anyone else was involved. A committee aide told CBS that the bureau had found no evidence that Jabbar had co-conspirators or was directed by a foreign actor or terrorist organisation, and that the attack was inspired by ISIS. He was not on any federal watchlist, the aide said. Islamic State had not claimed responsibility, NPR reported on the day. The day before, FBI assistant special agent in charge Alethea Duncan had said the bureau did not believe he was solely responsible, a view the FBI later dropped.

Later FBI statements added detail. Jabbar had become "more devout" in 2022 and began to follow extremist views in the spring of 2024, officials said, and he had travelled to Cairo, Egypt, from 22 June to 3 July 2023, and to Ontario, Canada, in July 2023. Investigators were still asking whom he met and associated with during the Cairo trip. In a press release reported on 14 January, the FBI said his internet history included searches on Bourbon Street balcony access, Mardi Gras and shootings in the city, and that hours before the attack he researched the Christmas-market ramming in Germany. FBI Director Christopher Wray told 60 Minutes that Jabbar was "radicalized online" and was determined to murder as many innocent people as he could "in the name of ISIS".

The FBI said Jabbar made two earlier trips to New Orleans, one beginning on 30 October 2024 and one on 10 November. On the first he recorded a bicycle ride through the French Quarter with Meta smart glasses. He picked up the truck in Houston on 30 December and drove to Louisiana on 31 December, according to FBI officials at a briefing. They said he stayed at a short-term rental on Mandeville Street, in the St. Roch area, which he set on fire before leaving, though the fire burned itself out. Investigators said he also left two improvised explosive devices in coolers in the French Quarter, which did not go off, and that other people who moved one of the coolers unaware of its contents were not seen as accomplices. Bomb-making materials were found at his Houston home and at the rental. The FBI said he wore the smart glasses during the attack but did not use them to livestream.

The attack at once raised the question of why a vehicle could enter the street. Mayor LaToya Cantrell said the bollards that normally block cars from Bourbon Street were not up because they were being replaced, with the work near completion ahead of the Super Bowl. Fox 8 reported that the city had begun that project a week after Jabbar's second visit. A police car had been serving as a makeshift roadblock, NPR reported, and Kirkpatrick said the wedge barriers on the street were known to malfunction: "We had a car there, we had barriers there, we had officers there, and he still got around."

She later acknowledged that the city owned vehicle barriers, called archers, that were not used, and said "I didn't know about them, but we have them." Fox 8 reported that Investigate TV found the city had used the same barriers for major events as far back as 2017. Governor Jeff Landry dismissed the "what-ifs" at a news conference and called the attack evil.

Kirkpatrick asked the former New York City police chief Bill Bratton and his consultancy to study how to protect the city, and Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill opened a state investigation. The City Council started a separate review of how the bollards had been chosen. In April 2025 Bratton's report recommended closing Bourbon Street to vehicles, which began a debate about public safety and neighbourhood access. On the first anniversary, Fox 8 reported that the street still opened to vehicles at set times, that new barriers were in place and that leaders were seeking a permanent solution. Murrill's office said it had completed its report and was in talks with the city, and that the city would release details of the findings as appropriate. The council's review was delayed and was expected in early 2026.

The Sugar Bowl at the Caesars Superdome was postponed by a day. President Joe Biden called the attack heinous and warned against jumping to conclusions. Officials examined whether it was connected to a Tesla Cybertruck that exploded outside a Trump hotel in Las Vegas that morning, Biden said. At Super Bowl LIX on 9 February, representatives of the police, EMS, fire and state agencies held photos of the 14 dead for the coin toss, and more than 2,700 officers from state, federal and local forces secured the game.
